source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Activate the facility fire plan, including alarm, relocation or evacuation, and assigned staff duties","B":"Use an improvised response because written emergency procedures are unnecessary during hospital fires","C":"Wait for the fire to spread before beginning evacuation or activating the facility emergency plan","D":"Treat the incident only as an external mass-casualty influx and ignore internal fire procedures"}}
source_row.rationale: The prior item relied on a loose 'internal versus external disaster' label. OSHA hospital fire-safety guidance instead supports a concrete emergency-action-plan response: reporting/alarm procedures, evacuation or escape routes, assigned duties, and trained personnel. CMS emergency preparedness likewise uses an all-hazards approach that includes fires and loss of facility operations.
source_row.source_detail: Hospital fire-safety guidance requires applicable emergency action planning; 29 CFR 1910.38 plan elements include reporting fires, evacuation procedures/escape routes, critical-operation duties, accountability, rescue/medical duties, and responsible contacts.
source_row.source_name: OSHA — Hospitals: Fire Safety and Emergency Action Plans
source_row.stem: A fire starts inside a hospital and threatens a patient-care area. Which principle should guide the unit's response?
